title: Americans Are Losing The Long Game | NOEMA
gist: Curtis and Klaus argue the US-China contest is decided not by frontier invention but by who can diffuse technology at scale and build transnational infrastructure over decades, and that America's short-termism and nostalgia have left it sitting out that long game while China executes it via the Belt and Road Initiative and its 15th Five-Year Plan. They point to the abundance agenda, a sovereign Strategic Investment Fund, Newsom's 'AI New Deal' ideas and Biden-era corridors like Lobito as templates for re-linking domestic renewal to international order.

themes.theme: US short-termism vs China's decades-long strategy

insights.claim: The authors argue the real US-China contest is not tariffs, military capabilities or even AI and clean energy, but a slower contest over who offers the most compelling vision of the future and can build it.
insights.speaker: SIMON CURTIS AND IAN KLAUS
insights.so_what: Suggests headline trade and tech skirmishes are noise relative to long-cycle infrastructure and institution-building positioning.
insights.quote: It is a deeper and slower contest over who offers the most compelling vision of the future, and who can bring that vision into being.

insights.claim: US political and economic culture is trapped in short cycles (two-year midterms, policy reversals between administrations, quarterly business cycles, 24-hour news), which the authors say curtails long-term investment and strategic continuity.
insights.speaker: SIMON CURTIS AND IAN KLAUS
insights.so_what: Policy whiplash raises the risk premium on long-duration US projects dependent on federal support.
insights.quote: quarterly business cycles that curtail long-term investment, 24-hour news cycles
insights.locator: But the roots of America's problems

insights.claim: The authors characterize MAGA's orientation as nostalgic and argue part of its failure in government stems from lacking a future-oriented domestic or international vision.
insights.speaker: SIMON CURTIS AND IAN KLAUS
insights.so_what: Frames the current administration's policy as unlikely to produce durable long-horizon industrial or alliance strategy.
insights.quote: Part of MAGA’s failure in government stems from its lack of a compelling future-oriented vision for either domestic or international society.

insights.claim: Rush Doshi's review of three decades of Chinese-language party and military documents found a consistent long-term Chinese effort to blunt and eventually displace US dominance, predating Xi Jinping.
insights.speaker: SIMON CURTIS AND IAN KLAUS
insights.so_what: Implies Chinese strategic direction is structural and unlikely to shift with leadership changes or trade deals.

insights.claim: China's 15th Five-Year Plan doubles down on state-planned investment in technology, infrastructure and dominance of critical supply chains, the strategy that has underpinned its rise for four decades.
insights.speaker: SIMON CURTIS AND IAN KLAUS
insights.so_what: Signals continued Chinese state capital flows into strategic sectors and supply-chain chokepoints.
insights.quote: In its recently unveiled 15th Five-Year Plan, Beijing doubled down on the industrial strategy of using state economic planning

insights.claim: If the US takes the wrong path, the authors predict its moment of primacy will have lasted about a century, a familiar historical pattern for great powers.
insights.speaker: SIMON CURTIS AND IAN KLAUS
insights.so_what: A long-horizon framing of hegemonic decline risk relevant to dollar and alliance-dependent assets.
insights.quote: If the wrong path is taken, then the moment of American primacy will have lasted about a century

insights.claim: Citing Jeffrey Ding, the authors argue great-power technology contests are won not by breakthrough inventions but by the patient, long-term diffusion of technology through infrastructure, training, institutions and reorganized production.
insights.speaker: SIMON CURTIS AND IAN KLAUS
insights.so_what: Shifts the investment lens from frontier-model leaders toward adoption enablers and deployment infrastructure.
insights.quote: technological contests between great powers are ultimately won not by breakthrough inventions but by the patient and long-term work of diffusion

insights.claim: The US holds a lead at the technological frontier (AI, advanced semiconductors, cloud, biotech, space launch, quantum) but has thought less about diffusion, while China is building the infrastructures of diffusion that may extract the greatest benefit from those innovations.
insights.speaker: SIMON CURTIS AND IAN KLAUS
insights.so_what: US frontier leadership may not translate into proportional economic or geopolitical returns.
insights.quote: Although the commanding heights of creativity and innovation may continue to reside in the U.S., China is building the infrastructures of diffusion

insights.claim: Silicon Valley's big labs fear that China's approach of opening its AI models to international partners could undermine the US closed-source proprietary model and expand Chinese influence in the global AI race.
insights.speaker: SIMON CURTIS AND IAN KLAUS
insights.so_what: Open-weight Chinese models threaten pricing power and global market share of US proprietary AI vendors.
insights.quote: The big labs of Silicon Valley are currently gripped by fear that China’s approach to opening its AI models to international partners may undermine the closed-source, proprietary model approach
insights.locator: The big labs of Silicon Valley

insights.claim: China already controls many critical supply chains for future technologies, including processed rare earths, batteries and robotics, which Jake Sullivan calls 'nodes of leverage' that blunted Trump's tariff pressure.
insights.speaker: SIMON CURTIS AND IAN KLAUS
insights.so_what: Rare earth and battery supply-chain chokepoints limit US tariff leverage and keep supply-security trades relevant.

insights.claim: In clean energy and biomedicine, the authors argue the US problem is not breakthroughs but lagging transmission, grid and deployment infrastructure due to a lack of state-driven investment and fragmented governance.
insights.speaker: SIMON CURTIS AND IAN KLAUS
insights.so_what: Points to grid and transmission build-out as the binding constraint and potential policy-driven opportunity.
insights.quote: America’s problem has never been the frontier, but the failure to deploy and diffuse technologies at scale in areas where markets alone have proven unable to coordinate collective action.
insights.locator: In many domains like clean energy

themes.theme: Belt and Road as geopolitical infrastructure

insights.claim: Over 13 years China's Belt and Road Initiative has built rail, road, maritime, digital, energy transmission and smart-city networks that steer flows of resources, goods, people and influence toward China.
insights.speaker: SIMON CURTIS AND IAN KLAUS
insights.so_what: Control of transnational infrastructure gives China structural leverage over resource and trade flows across Eurasia and Africa.
insights.quote: By building infrastructure and shaping cities far beyond its borders, China is working to ensure that momentum is angled toward its own growing center of gravity.

insights.claim: AI and an alternative internet carried over Belt and Road digital infrastructure are, per the authors, enrolling states across Eurasia and Africa into China's sociotechnical system.
insights.speaker: SIMON CURTIS AND IAN KLAUS
insights.so_what: Suggests a bifurcating global tech stack with Chinese standards locked in across emerging markets.
insights.quote: Artificial intelligence and an alternative internet are enrolling states into China’s enlarging sociotechnical system across Eurasia and Africa.

insights.claim: The authors acknowledge China faces an aging population, a growing debt burden, an extended property-sector crisis, weak soft power and few allies, and its centralization could become a weakness.
insights.speaker: SIMON CURTIS AND IAN KLAUS
insights.so_what: Balances the thesis: China's long game carries real macro and political execution risks.
insights.quote: China has an aging population, a burgeoning debt cloud, an extended property sector crisis and still lacks genuine soft power and allies.
insights.locator: There are challenges to be sure.

themes.theme: Lost US advantages: domestic-foreign linkage and alliances

insights.claim: The authors argue the US has lost two long-held strategic advantages: linking its domestic agenda to foreign policy to enable intergenerational investment, and a robust network of allies and institutions to project power.
insights.speaker: SIMON CURTIS AND IAN KLAUS
insights.so_what: Erosion of alliances reduces US access to the dispersed critical minerals, energy and talent needed for AI and clean energy.

insights.claim: The Inflation Reduction Act was the hinge between Biden's domestic and international programs, aiming to turn the Rust Belt into a 'cobalt corridor', but it stalled and was decisively reversed in places after Trump's return.
insights.speaker: SIMON CURTIS AND IAN KLAUS
insights.so_what: Policy reversal of IRA support undermines green-energy investment certainty in post-industrial US regions.

insights.claim: Biden-era projects like the Lobito Trans-Africa Corridor (linking Angola's port to critical-mineral regions of the DRC and Zambia) and the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor copied China's playbook but relied on private finance rather than direct state investment, and the US moved away from this approach after the change in administration.
insights.speaker: SIMON CURTIS AND IAN KLAUS
insights.so_what: Western critical-mineral corridor projects in Africa face reduced US political backing, weakening alternatives to Chinese supply.
insights.quote: The big difference was the central role of private-sector finance, rather than direct state investment as in the Chinese model.

themes.theme: Paths to renewal: abundance, project-state, AI New Deal

insights.claim: The authors invoke Charles Maier's 'Project-State' concept, arguing China today more closely resembles history-making project-states than a US hollowed out by market ideology and populism.
insights.speaker: SIMON CURTIS AND IAN KLAUS
insights.so_what: Frames state capacity and mission-driven industrial policy as decisive in hegemonic competition.
insights.quote: The project-state, by its very nature, plays a long game.
insights.locator: The project-state, by its very nature

insights.claim: The authors endorse the abundance agenda of Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson as a template beyond laissez-faire, diagnosing red tape, legalism, polarization and lost state building capacity as what blocks US deployment.
insights.speaker: SIMON CURTIS AND IAN KLAUS
insights.so_what: Permitting reform and state-capacity politics could become a post-MAGA policy direction affecting infrastructure and energy build-outs.
insights.locator: America’s ability to construct a future

insights.claim: The authors propose a sovereign infrastructure institution such as a Strategic Investment Fund to de-risk long-term projects and unlock private capital so the US and allies can match the scale of Belt and Road.
insights.speaker: SIMON CURTIS AND IAN KLAUS
insights.so_what: A potential new public-private vehicle for infrastructure capital deployment if adopted by a future administration.
insights.quote: One missing policy mechanism is a sovereign infrastructure institution, such as a Strategic Investment Fund, that could unlock private capital
insights.locator: At its heart is a politics

insights.claim: California Governor Gavin Newsom has issued executive orders on safety nets for AI-displaced workers, including subsidies to retain and upskill employees and exploring 'universal basic capital' stakes in asset funds, and his progressive backers favor an 'AI New Deal'.
insights.speaker: SIMON CURTIS AND IAN KLAUS
insights.so_what: Previews possible national AI labor-displacement policy if Newsom wins the 2028 Democratic nomination.

insights.claim: If Newsom gains the 2028 Democratic nomination, the authors suggest his California approach could become a subnational model scaled to national and international policy.
insights.speaker: SIMON CURTIS AND IAN KLAUS
insights.so_what: Signals how a Democratic administration might regulate and redistribute AI gains after 2028.

insights.claim: The authors argue great powers are judged ultimately not by wealth or weapons but by the futures they can persuade others to inhabit.
insights.speaker: SIMON CURTIS AND IAN KLAUS
insights.so_what: Soft power and order-building capacity are framed as the long-run determinant of geopolitical alignment.
insights.quote: Great powers are ultimately judged not by the wealth they accumulate or the weapons they possess, but by the futures they can persuade others to inhabit.
